Let’s talk about something that goes deeper than just money, or finding a quiet corner to work.
Chapter Four: The Weight of Expectations and the Struggle for Authenticity.
You know, once you start looking past the outside world—past the dollars and the distractions—there’s a whole other challenge waiting. It’s the expectations we all carry around. The ones that shape how women see themselves, and how the world sees them.
Think about it. From the time girls are little, they’re told to be agreeable. To put everyone else first. Don’t draw too much attention, don’t make waves.
And honestly, the world seems to reward those who fit in, who play by the rules, who keep the peace.
For anyone who dreams of writing, those lessons are tough to unlearn. That fear of being judged—of being called unfeminine, or even ungrateful—it can get in the way of saying what really matters.
There’s this story I want to share—a young woman, trying to write about her own life and what she wants. But every time she sits down to put her thoughts on paper, she hesitates. She starts editing herself before the words even make it out.
She can’t help but wonder: what will her family think? What will her friends say? Will anyone even take her seriously?
Suddenly, writing isn’t just about telling the truth. It’s about walking a tightrope—balancing her real self with what she believes people expect from her.
Most folks don’t realize just how much energy goes into this kind of second-guessing. Every sentence is measured, every idea questioned.
And what comes out?
Sometimes, it’s just a watered-down version—a voice trying so hard to please everyone, it ends up not saying much at all.
There’s advice everywhere: what to write, how to write, who your writing should be for. But here’s something to pay attention to—the most important lesson is also the hardest. Learning to trust your own voice. To write what feels real, even if it’s not what people want to hear.
That’s not just about courage. It’s survival.
Because if you lose your authenticity, if you stop being true to yourself, then writing loses its meaning.
But then—there’s a moment of clarity. A feeling that the only way forward is to let go of needing approval.
The stories that matter most are the ones that come from real honesty, from vulnerability, from genuine experience.
The world might not always be ready to listen, but speaking out—sharing your truth—that’s powerful in itself.
The struggle for authenticity? It never really ends. The world’s expectations change slowly, and the pressure to fit in is always there.
But each time someone tells their story, each time a voice rises up and says, “This is who I am”—the path gets a little smoother for the next person who comes along.
